newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech high caps hit yr-lows in cloud of pessimism.
newsitem.headline: Czech high caps hit yr-lows in cloud of pessimism.

text.p: Bearish sentiment fuelled by a slumping Czech economy and expectations of poor company earnings pushed several blue chips to year-lows on Tuesday, with dealers predicting more losses to come.

SPT Telecom fell 5.8 percent to 3,054 crowns, while power utility CEZ dropped 3.8 percent to 904 crowns and Komercni Banka lost 3.5 percent 2,000 crowns, pulling the PSE's PX50 index down 2.7 percent to 508.0.
Taken together the three issues account for 45 percent of the index's total capitalisation and have a decisive influence on the direction of the market.
Pessimistic sentiment has enveloped the Czech equity market since early autumn 1996 when concerns about poor capital market regulation began to sap foreign investors' confidence.

However, despite a new commitment from the government to create a U.S-style Securities and Exchange Commission, analysts now say that other problems have surfaced making a quick upturn, especially in the major issues, very unlikely.

"There are three factors combined: One is still the trustworthiness of the Czech market...(Second) on the macro level we still see a lot of concerns...and third is that earnings are very disappointing," said Jan Sykora of Wood and Company.

The three issues, which attract the most interest from foreign investors, have all seen earnings fall in the first quarter, although analysts were generally more optimistic about SPT Telecom saying higher depreciation costs had distorted the true state of the company's earnings.
SPT saw pre-tax profits for the first three months of the year fall to 2.6 billion crowns from 2.8 billion in same period in 1996.

Komercni Banka's first quarter gross profit fell to one billion crowns from 1.3 billion and CEZ, the worst performer of the three, posted first quarter pre-tax profits of 4.9 billion crowns from 6.0 billion.
The development of earnings in the three companies is seen as reflective of the sectors of the economy in which they are involved.
Analysts said CEZ's fortunes have fallen in tandem with the sharp slowdown in industrial production which fell 5.8 percent year-on-year in February and 3.9 percent in January.

Komercni's prospects have been determined by the tightness of monetary policy and the high cost of borrowing -- the discount rate was raised last summer to 10.5 percent from 9.5 percent -- and SPT has been making heavy investments to modernise the dilapidated Czech telephone system.

The performance of the respective sectors has taken place in an envirnment characterised by falling economic growth. In 1996 gross domestic product rose by 4.4 percent from 4.8 percent the year before and the government recently slashed its 1997 GDP forecast to less than 2.7 percent from 5.4 percent.
In such circumstances, dealers questioned by Reuters said the major issues were likely to decline further.
"It's anybody's guess but I wouldn't be so surprised to see them (the afore-mentioned shares) take the market down another 10-20 percent," said one local dealer.
